\section*{Overview}
The supplement reports every configuration behind the main text, together with the controls and selection steps that
the article summarises in a sentence. All tables were generated by \path{scripts/make_supplement.py} from the files
frozen at repository tag \texttt{v0.9.5-results-frozen} and archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23601090), so each value can be traced to a hashed table or to a run of
a frozen grid. Seeds 1 to 5 give every reported mean, seed 0 serves only for selection, and intervals are two-sided
95\% $t$-intervals over seeds unless a caption states otherwise.

The sections follow the order of the article. Section S1 documents the duplicate check that defines the clean test set,
Section S2 compares the full and the clean test sets and adds the source controls, Section S3 gives the privacy
accounting and the selection costs, Section S4 covers client count and drift correction, Section S5 adds the
membership-inference detail, Section S6 the explanation detail and Section S7 the composition-matched attack and the
per-class sensitivity. Tables S5, S9 and S11 use the full test set of 813
images, and the clean-set values of the corresponding results come from Table S3.

\section{Benchmark curation and near-duplicate check}
Perceptual hashing removed exact and near-exact copies during curation, yet it compares images in one orientation
only. A second check therefore computed the normalised cross-correlation (NCC) between every pair of curated images at
$64\times64$ pixels, once as stored and once with one image mirrored, keeping the larger value. Part A
(Table~\ref{tab:s_ncc}) counts pairs above three thresholds and breaks the cross-split pairs down by the splits they
join.

\input{tables/ncc.tex}

At the threshold of 0.95, fixed before the check, 148 pairs crossed a split boundary and 120 of them matched only after
mirroring. Part B (Table~\ref{tab:s_ncc_b}) compares each duplicate removed during curation with the image it was
merged into. Pairs removed at Hamming distance 0 and 2 are confirmed, with 19 of 3678 below NCC 0.90, whereas 80 of the
296 pairs at distance 4 fall below 0.90, many of them SARTAJ copies of Figshare slices with a different crop that NCC
on whole images cannot align. Figure~\ref{fig:s_montage} shows the most similar cross-split pairs, most of them Br35H
no-tumour images whose mirrored twin sat in another split.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\textwidth]{top_cross_split_pairs.png}
\caption{Cross-split pairs with the highest NCC after mirroring.}
\label{fig:s_montage}
\end{figure}

\section{Full and clean test sets, and source controls}
Table~\ref{tab:s_full_clean} lists balanced accuracy for every reported configuration on the full and on the clean test
set, where sens$_N$ denotes no-tumour sensitivity. Removing the contaminated images changed configuration means by $-0.049$ to $+0.007$, mostly through lower
no-tumour sensitivity once the mirrored Br35H twins left the test set, and no qualitative conclusion of the
article changed.

\input{tables/full_clean.tex}

Local-only training (Table~\ref{tab:s_local}) shows what each client of the natural partition achieves alone. The Br35H
client holds no tumour images and cannot exceed the chance level of 0.25, and even the large Figshare client reaches at
most 0.625, below every non-private federated model.

\input{tables/local.tex}

The per-source controls in Table~\ref{tab:s_sources} separate source composition from diagnostic skill, with
specificity defined as no-tumour recall within one source. SARTAJ is the
only source with all four classes, and its four-class balanced accuracy stays below the pooled value in every setting
that learns more than chance. The pooled number therefore benefits from sources that hold only one or two classes.

\input{tables/sources.tex}

The probe in Table~\ref{tab:s_probe} tests whether penultimate features reveal the source collection within one class,
Figshare against SARTAJ among tumour images and SARTAJ against Br35H among no-tumour images.
Trained models decode the source only slightly better than an ImageNet-initialised network and a random network, so the
source signal is already present in the images before training.

\input{tables/probe.tex}

\section{Privacy accounting and selection cost}
Table~\ref{tab:s_eps} gives the accounted privacy loss of every private configuration. Federated learning rates were
chosen among two candidates trained on the same records, and composing the guarantee over both candidates raises
record-level $\varepsilon=8$ to 11.98, following the analysis of Papernot and Steinke for hyperparameter search. The
worst-unit $\varepsilon$ composes a patient-level guarantee over the clients that hold one unit.

\input{tables/eps.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:s_lr} lists the learning-rate candidates at seed 0 and the one selected by lowest validation loss. Every
non-private configuration selected 0.01, while most private ones selected 0.003, consistent with the smaller steps that
noisy gradients tolerate.

\input{tables/lr.tex}

\section{Client count and drift correction}
Table~\ref{tab:s_h5} holds the client-count experiment on Dirichlet ($\alpha=0.5$) partitions, with learning rate 0.003
under DP and 0.01 without, and aggregated noise $\sigma C\sqrt{K}/(qN)$ for $N=2610$. The aggregated noise standard deviation grows with $\sqrt{K}$
at a fixed noise multiplier, and accuracy at $\varepsilon=3$ falls as it grows, whereas accuracy without privacy shows
no trend.

\input{tables/h5.tex}

FedProx screening at seed 0 (Table~\ref{tab:s_fedprox}) shows that proximal weights of 0.01 and 0.1 change validation
loss by at most 0.0098. Larger weights lowered the loss in a few private settings and raised it elsewhere, without a
consistent pattern that would justify carrying FedProx to the seed runs.

\input{tables/fedprox.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:s_scaffold} compares size-weighted SCAFFOLD with FedAvg. No difference survives Holm correction, and the
uniform server average of the original algorithm collapses on unequal clients under privacy, most visibly on the
natural partition, where one client holds 2029 of the 2610 training images (77.7\%).

\input{tables/scaffold.tex}

\section{Membership inference}
The weight-noise comparator used a rule fixed before any seed run. Table~\ref{tab:s_wn} shows that the published
$s=0.5$ diverged, and that the rule selected $s=0.003$ as the largest level whose validation loss did not exceed that of
record-level $\varepsilon=8$.

\input{tables/wn.tex}

Tables~\ref{tab:s_week07_clean_lira} and \ref{tab:s_week07_lira} report LiRA with the clean and with the full test set
as non-members, in its online and its offline form. The choice of non-member set changes no conclusion, since online
AUC, true-positive rate at 1\% false positives and patient AUC move by less than 0.01 for every target that produced a
usable model. Section S7 tests whether the rates that remain under privacy exceed chance once members and non-members
are matched in composition.

\input{tables/lira.tex}

The loss-threshold attack in Table~\ref{tab:s_loss_mia} scores each image by its negative loss, and its within-stratum
AUC averages the AUC inside each source and class stratum. It is far weaker than LiRA even without privacy. Under privacy its
within-stratum AUC ranges from 0.458 to 0.507, so its values below 0.5 do not arise from the mix of sources and classes
in each split.

\input{tables/loss_mia.tex}

\section{Explanations}
Table~\ref{tab:s_xai} reports localisation and faithfulness for Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++ and Integrated Gradients across the
privacy settings of central training. Grad-CAM shows the clearest decline as the privacy budget shrinks, Grad-CAM++
declines more gently, and Integrated Gradients reaches the highest pointing rate without privacy, a result that the
randomisation check qualifies.

\input{tables/xai.tex}

The randomisation check in Table~\ref{tab:s_rand} decides which method deserves interpretation, re-initialising
either all layers or only the last block and classifier of central seed-1 models on 64 images. Integrated Gradients
with a black baseline keeps a rank correlation of 0.683 to 0.712 with maps from a network whose weights were all
re-initialised, so its maps mostly reflect the input image, whereas Grad-CAM correlations stay between $-0.047$ and
0.388. The check used one seed per setting and 64 images, which separates the two methods but does not rank privacy
settings.

\input{tables/rand.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:s_border} tests for skull-border and background artefacts, adds Grad-CAM from the third residual block
at twice the resolution and lists the cross-seed consistency used in the article. Grad-CAM places less mass on the
brain rim and outside the brain than their area shares, so neither artefact explains the localisation results.

\input{tables/border.tex}

Table~\ref{tab:s_mediation} relates explanation quality to accuracy and noise, once per model and once per
configuration, where each point is the mean over the seeds of one configuration (five for central and three for
federated configurations). Seeds of one configuration share the mean map against which consistency is measured, so
the configuration level is the conservative analysis. Both metrics correlate with clean balanced accuracy at both
levels, and the noise multiplier adds no explanatory power once accuracy is in the fit.

\input{tables/mediation.tex}

\section{Composition-matched membership inference and per-class sensitivity}
Removing the 66 contaminated test images changed the mix of the non-members. Br35H forms 230 of 2610 members (8.8\%)
but 6 of 747 clean non-members (0.8\%), and no-tumour images form 432 of 2610 members (16.6\%) against 60 of 747
non-members (8.0\%). A score that only recognises the source or class of an image can then separate the two groups.
Table~\ref{tab:s_matched} therefore repeats the online LiRA of Table~\ref{tab:s_week07_clean_lira} with the same
shadow fits in three ways, namely with all clean non-members, with non-members reweighted so that their source and
class mix equals that of the members, and with both groups restricted to Figshare and reweighted by class. The
effective sample size (ESS) gives the number of equally weighted non-members that carries the same information.

\input{tables/matched.tex}

Under privacy, only the unmatched rate at $\varepsilon=8$ differs significantly from the nominal 0.01 (one-sample
$t$-test over five targets, two-sided), and no matched or Figshare-only rate does. The diverged weight-noise models at
$s=0.5$ classify at chance, yet they reach rates of 0.024 to 0.039, so rates of a few percent at 1\% false positives
can arise in this audit without a usable classifier. The $p$-values are descriptive and not corrected for multiple
comparisons.

Table~\ref{tab:s_class} breaks clean balanced accuracy into the recall of each class, recomputed from the stored
predictions of every reported run.

\input{tables/class.tex}
